Gwala Ka Jan - A Pollsmoor Production

By: Marion Edmunds | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We see how creative writing and acting can set convicted prisoners free

Unique Selling Point:
We have unique access to a writing and theatre project inside Pollsmoor prison, thanks to the intervention of creative writing teacher Dr Suzette Leal who has been teaching prisoners creative writing, to the extent that they have developed a semi-autobiographical play which is to be performed for friends and family from outside the prison.

Summary:
Gwala Ka Jan – A Pollsmoor Production
When a convict enters a new prison in South Africa he is asked Gwala Ka Jan? Which is the lingo for: Who are you? His or her answer will determine where he sleeps, who he associates with and where he sits in the prison hierarchy.
Gwala Ka Jan is the name of a play developed by Pollsmoor offenders with the help of a creative writing teacher, Suzette Leal, who volunteered earlier this year at the prison, not quite knowing how drawn into the lives of individual convicts she would become. Nor did she know that the “narrative therapy” she was using would become not only a lifeline, but the foundation for a play, written by prisoners, starring prisoners and engaging an audience from outside of the prison walls. It’s not been done before in South Africa.
To capture both the interaction between a relatively wealthy woman and three prisoners, as well as to explore the success of narrative therapy, we have been given permission to go inside Pollsmoor, under the watchful eye of Correctional Services.
We have asked to interview three prisoners who are part of the play.
Characters:
• Curt Vincer, artist, recovering addict in prison for murdering his grandmother
• Fareed Pelton, senior general of 27 gang, convicted murderer, serving time for breaking parole, trying to retire from the Number
• Mdu, professional opera singer who is serving time for housebreaking (itv not quite guaranteed yet)

They will talk about their backgrounds, what got them into prison, the impact of Narrative Therapy, and how the play has taken shape. They will talk of how they want the play to impact the audience, and the wider public. We will touch on the themes of identity, rehabilitation versus punishment and the tension between physical incarceration and imaginative freedom. We will ask them what it is like to be in prison, about their routines, and the world it creates around them. We will have to be sensitive of how much they want to tell us about the crimes they committed – I have been told that Curt is very sensitive and unsure whether he wants to reveal the whole story.

We will also see them doing the things that make them special. We will film Curt drawing, and being the librarian at Medium B. I attach some of his pictures. We film Fareed writing in class with Suzette Leal who has engaged them in her class since March this year. We film Mdu singing. (Shades of the Shawshank Redemption)

We will also film them all in dress rehearsal with Natasha Dryden, a former Sewende Laan actress who is helping them get the play ready. We will interview Natasha in the recreational hall once the dress rehearsal is done, so that she can reflect on what she is able to teach them and what she has experienced directing this play.

We are obliged to interview a Correctional Services representative. They can’t decide who but will tell us in time as the person “needs to be prepared”. Correctional Services is in the process of trying to rebrand themselves as a more loving, caring rehabilitative institution. The week before the play, 300 warders and offenders are travelling to George (where John is) for a literary festival which will include a Spelling Bee in all the official languages, including Nama. I have asked for some visuals of this, to flesh out the theme of rehabilitation as opposed to punishment, as well as to strategically signal to DCS that we are on their side. Suzette tells me that most of the prisoners seem to while away their time sleeping, so the literary festival is in stark contrast to the default slumber.

Then we will leave the prison to go “outside” to Camps Bay where Suzette lives. We will interview her there, and maybe get B-roll of her on the beach. I would want to capture visuals of “freedom” – beach, sea, palm trees in the wind etc as a contrast to the prison interior.

Then we will return to Medium B on the night of one of the performances. I have asked for the camera to be back stage, to catch the nerves of the actors – those who can murder and housebreak but are nervous about standing up and saying their lines in front of an audience. We will capture them asking the audience the question: Gwala Ka Jan? and then also the applause at the end. This will make the shoot longer but seeing it is in the same week as our interviews, I think it is worth getting it. It should count as another half day.

All of this has been signed off in principle by Correctional Services.

Press Release:


Gwala Ka Jan: A Pollsmoor Production
When a convict enters a prison in South Africa he is asked, “Gwala Ka Jan?” – lingo for “Who are you?” The answer will determine where he sleeps, with whom he associates, and where he sits in the prison hierarchy. But now, Gwala ka Jan is also the title of a semi-autobiographical play developed by inmates of Pollsmoor Prison. It’s a South African first; a story about identity, rehabilitation, punishment, and the tension between physical incarceration and imaginative freedom. And, as men who have murdered and robbed master their stage fright, Carte Blanche goes backstage.
Producer: Marion Edmunds | Presenter: Masa Kekana


Script:


Gwala Ka Jan – Rudi’s Studio script 6793

(Masa) In Cape Town, Pollsmoor Maximum Security Prison holds many dark secrets.
For over half a century, generations of convicts have done time here. Their shared challenge is navigating the unique South African prison gang system known as The Number, a highly secretive and violent organisation.

(Masa) I have never been to a prison before, and coming into Pollsmoor I was quite nervous. And now being inside here, I’m still nervous, it’s rough in here.

(Masa) We were given unprecedented access to this aging jail - a rare opportunity to be on the other side of the notorious walls of Pollsmoor.

(Masa) Long-time offender Faried Pelton remembers his arrival here. He was only 16 when he first faced the prison gangs.

(Faried Pelton) They were like on top of you, it's like they’re predators. And then you have that mentality of either you man up, you face your fears, because you can't let these people break you.

(Masa) Faried climbed the gang ranks over time. Now, he and a small group of offenders have written a play which gives us a glimpse into this experience. It’s called Gwala Ka Jan - which is prison lingo for: who are you?

(Prisoner One) Gwala ka jan? Gwala ka jan? I say who the f*** are you?

(Keegan) I’m, I’m Keegan.

(Masa) This question, Gwala Ka Jan, is put to any new inmate when they first step into their cell.

(Prisoner One Subtitles) Now listen here, this is not your mother’s f***ing house.

(Prisoner Two Subtitles) Or your father’s f***ing farm.

(Prisoner One Subtitles) Or your granny’s f***ing hotel.

(Keegan Subtitles) Yessir.

(Upsound Keegan) I like how the boy keeps searching.

(Masa) The answer to Gwala Ka Jan will set up the offender for years to come, either within the brutal hierarchy of the gangs - the 26s, 27s or 28s - or, as a subservient inmate called a Frans. Offender, Curt Vincer, act’s the play’s lead.

(Curt Vincer) It's a life in prison. It's our experience. And the whole thing is basically the story of a Frans like me now, a new one, coming into the system, where you don't have any power here. Yes, you submit to the to the wardens but when these gates close and they go home, you will submit under The Number, and that's where things go.

(Masa) Veteran warden, Captain Brandon Verrooi, has seen inmates come and go over four decades. He knows prison lore.
(Brandon Verrooi) You need to follow the rules of the of the gangsters now. You sleep, you know, you sleep in the corner, there's no bed for you. You are a cleaner, you do the washing, so you've got no say.

(General Subtitles) You! It’s not cleaned well, wash it again!

(Masa) Who sets the rules?

(Brandon Verrooi) The gangsters set the rules.

(Masa Kekana) Down these dark corridors, Verrooi found talent. He encouraged an opera singer who had been convicted of theft to join the cast. Mdu Semanu has been in and out of prison for almost twenty years but he is still haunted by the question on his first day: Gwala Ka Jan?

(Mdu Semanu) Ah. Oh, it was so tense and I was so freaky scared, just because it was my first experience.

(Masa) Ja.

(Mdu Semanu) Yes.

(Masa) Do you remember what you answered? What did you say when you were asked?

(Mdu Semanu) I did told them that I'm a Frans.

(Brandon Verrooi) So Gwala Ka Jan is a powerful term that's going to take us right into the play. And certainly you can have to make a choice whether you a gangster or you're not. So it's a story that carries you into the world of the gangster, how to choose or not to choose.

(Masa) But the play would not have come to life if it hadn’t been for an unconventional academic. Dr Suzette Leal volunteered to hold weekly creative writing courses at Pollsmoor, not realising where they would lead.

(Suzette Leal) For the most part, it's writing about their own lives and their own feelings. But it's mostly childhood trauma, I'd say, yeah.

(Masa) Suzette witnessed her students grapple with their crimes, and their past lives.

(Upsound Suzette Leal) I want you to tell me how do you think people see you and how do you see yourself?

(Masa) They poured their pain into words. Faried grew up without a father on the Cape Flats and as a teenager was unable to dodge the crossfire.

(Faried Pelton) My brother got shot and killed. I went to the gang and to I went to go look for a gun, started shooting back, and that life put me in and out of prison.

(Masa) Curt, an artist convicted of murder, has blossomed under Suzette’s mentorship.

(Curt Vincer) It taught me how to channel my frustrations, not just on people, but to watch yourself and really sit and listen to yourself. And if you can't, if you're not comfortable with talking to people, pick up a pen.

(Masa) Writing through trauma started a slow journey to healing, in the tiny library at Medium B.

(Suzette Leal) I can see a willingness to be vulnerable. I can see reduced aggression, reduced violence. I get feed-back also about what happens on the unit when there’s conflict. In terms of behaviour that I’ve observed, I've definitely seen a change.

(Curt Vincer) My library does distract me. No, it does - is some form of escape to get out of the system for a bit. But there's times when you do come to your own stillness in your room, wherever, and even reading a book, something can just trigger that memory. And I'm in this fucking place because of my own crime, to- towards my family, it will never let me go.

(Masa) Razor wire, locks and bars deprive convicts of their freedom – it’s the ultimate punishment for serious crime. But should coming here be the end of their story, or a chance to write a new beginning.

Upsound Faried: No, I am good at maths now.
Upsound Suzette: Yes

(Masa) Their play grew from a script to the stage, facilitated by Suzette and Warden Verrooi.

(Brandon Verrooi) It was so nice to see a group of people sitting with the same hurt and not being being shy to talk to one another, going through trauma from childhood, how they ended up in gangsterism.

(Masa) Mid-rehearsal comes a smoke break. Shooting the breeze, feeling fresh air. And then back to work with acting coach and director, Natasha Dryden.

(Upsound Natasha Dryden) What I want to say is that we are going to be brilliant.

(Upsound Prisoner) Oh yeah!

(Masa) An actor herself, Natasha has taught the group the art of stage-craft.

(Natasha Dryden) In theatre, the stakes are high. It's live.

(Upsound Prisoner) Salute!

(Upsound Prisoner) Salute!

(Natasha Dryden) There's a massive trust-building that also happens in that process.

(Masa Kekana) What's been the most difficult part of all of this for you?

(Natasha Dryden) Possibly confronting my own pre-judgments. Being able to see the humanity behind the criminal.

(Upsound Natasha Dryden) Entry was stunning, and you know what, I have a very nice idea….

(Masa) We are just a few days away from opening night and the entire production – from the cast, to the crew and technical team have put themselves under huge pressure to make sure this performance is an exceptional experience.

(Masa) Mdu is the only actor here who is used to being on stage.
In the play, he sings a moving solo while the prisoners beat up Keegan, the Frans, who eventually capitulates and joins The Number.

(Upsound Prisoner, singing) Then sings my soul, my Saviour God, to Thee

(Keegan Subtitles) I am ready to join, sir.
(The General Subtitles) Are you sure?
(Keegan Subtitles) Yes, sir! I am sure.

(Upsound General, incantation) Salute!

(Prisoners) Salute!

(Masa) Playing to a full house, this prison-drama is a thriller, true to it’s genre.

(Masa) For just for a few hours, this Correctional Services Facility in Cape Town will be a stage and the prisoners the players. This is a Pollsmoor production.

(Masa) Instead of stabbing a warder, the character Keegan murders the General, in a plot twist which takes everybody by surprise.

(Brandon Verrooi) This play will really be an eye-opener for us, most of the DCS people as well, and I'm sure that we're going to use it to train people.

(Masa) The curtain will fall and the actors become prisoners again.
But the written word has shown its power.

(Faried Pelton) And I promise to myself that I'm not coming back to this place. I rather make that turn and try to give back to the community, and try to keep the children away from this place, because this place was made for people, but it's not a place for people.

(Masa) Veteran warden, Captain Brandon Verrooi, has seen inmates come and go over four decades. He knows prison lore. (Brandon Verrooi) You need to follow the rules of the of the gangsters now. You sleep, you know, you sleep in the corner, there's no bed for you. You are a cleaner, you do the washing, so you've got no say. (General Subtitles) You! It’s not cleaned well, wash it again! (Masa) Who sets the rules? (Brandon Verrooi) The gangsters set the rules. (Masa Kekana) Down these dark corridors, Verrooi found talent. He encouraged an opera singer who had been convicted of theft to join the cast. Mdu Semanu has been in and out of prison for almost twenty years but he is still haunted by the question on his first day: Gwala Ka Jan? (Mdu Semanu) Ah. Oh, it was so tense and I was so freaky scared, just because it was my first experience. (Masa) Ja. (Mdu Semanu) Yes. (Masa) Do you remember what you answered? What did you say when you were asked? (Mdu Semanu) I did told them that I'm a Frans. (Brandon Verrooi) So Gwala Ka Jan is a powerful term that's going to take us right into the play. And certainly you can have to make a choice whether you a gangster or you're not. So it's a story that carries you into the world of the gangster, how to choose or not to choose. (Masa) But the play would not have come to life if it hadn’t been for an unconventional academic. Dr Suzette Leal volunteered to hold weekly creative writing courses at Pollsmoor, not realising where they would lead. (Suzette Leal) For the most part, it's writing about their own lives and their own feelings. But it's mostly childhood trauma, I'd say, yeah. (Masa) Suzette witnessed her students grapple with their crimes, and their past lives. (Upsound Suzette Leal) I want you to tell me how do you think people see you and how do you see yourself? (Masa) They poured their pain into words. Faried grew up without a father on the Cape Flats and as a teenager was unable to dodge the crossfire. (Faried Pelton) My brother got shot and killed. I went to the gang and to I went to go look for a gun, started shooting back, and that life put me in and out of prison. (Masa) Curt, an artist convicted of murder, has blossomed under Suzette’s mentorship. (Curt Vincer) It taught me how to channel my frustrations, not just on people, but to watch yourself and really sit and listen to yourself. And if you can't, if you're not comfortable with talking to people, pick up a pen. (Masa) Writing through trauma started a slow journey to healing, in the tiny library at Medium B. (Suzette Leal) I can see a willingness to be vulnerable. I can see reduced aggression, reduced violence. I get feed-back also about what happens on the unit when there’s conflict. In terms of behaviour that I’ve observed, I've definitely seen a change. (Curt Vincer) My library does distract me. No, it does - is some form of escape to get out of the system for a bit. But there's times when you do come to your own stillness in your room, wherever, and even reading a book, something can just trigger that memory. And I'm in this fucking place because of my own crime, to- towards my family, it will never let me go. (Masa) Razor wire, locks and bars deprive convicts of their freedom – it’s the ultimate punishment for serious crime. But should coming here be the end of their story, or a chance to write a new beginning. Upsound Faried: No, I am good at maths now. Upsound Suzette: Yes (Masa) Their play grew from a script to the stage, facilitated by Suzette and Warden Verrooi. (Brandon Verrooi) It was so nice to see a group of people sitting with the same hurt and not being being shy to talk to one another, going through trauma from childhood, how they ended up in gangsterism. (Masa) Mid-rehearsal comes a smoke break. Shooting the breeze, feeling fresh air. And then back to work with acting coach and director, Natasha Dryden. (Upsound Natasha Dryden) What I want to say is that we are going to be brilliant. (Upsound Prisoner) Oh yeah! (Masa) An actor herself, Natasha has taught the group the art of stage-craft. (Natasha Dryden) In theatre, the stakes are high. It's live. (Upsound Prisoner) Salute! (Upsound Prisoner) Salute! (Natasha Dryden) There's a massive trust-building that also happens in that process. (Masa Kekana) What's been the most difficult part of all of this for you? (Natasha Dryden) Possibly confronting my own pre-judgments. Being able to see the humanity behind the criminal. (Upsound Natasha Dryden) Entry was stunning, and you know what, I have a very nice idea…. (Masa) We are just a few days away from opening night and the entire production – from the cast, to the crew and technical team have put themselves under huge pressure to make sure this performance is an exceptional experience. (Masa) Mdu is the only actor here who is used to being on stage. In the play, he sings a moving solo while the prisoners beat up Keegan, the Frans, who eventually capitulates and joins The Number. (Upsound Prisoner, singing) Then sings my soul, my Saviour God, to Thee (Keegan Subtitles) I am ready to join, sir. (The General Subtitles) Are you sure? (Keegan Subtitles) Yes, sir! I am sure. (Upsound General, incantation) Salute! (Prisoners) Salute! (Masa) Playing to a full house, this prison-drama is a thriller, true to it’s genre. (Masa) For just for a few hours, this Correctional Services Facility in Cape Town will be a stage and the prisoners the players. This is a Pollsmoor production. (Masa) Instead of stabbing a warder, the character Keegan murders the General, in a plot twist which takes everybody by surprise. (Brandon Verrooi) This play will really be an eye-opener for us, most of the DCS people as well, and I'm sure that we're going to use it to train people. (Masa) The curtain will fall and the actors become prisoners again. But the written word has shown its power. (Faried Pelton) And I promise to myself that I'm not coming back to this place. I rather make that turn and try to give back to the community, and try to keep the children away from this place, because this place was made for people, but it's not a place for people.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We see how creative writing and acting can set convicted prisoners free
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We have unique access to a writing and theatre project inside Pollsmoor prison, thanks to the intervention of creative writing teacher Dr Suzette Leal who has been teaching prisoners creative writing, to the extent that they have developed a semi-autobiographical play which is to be performed for friends and family from outside the prison.
metadata.Summary: Gwala Ka Jan – A Pollsmoor Production When a convict enters a new prison in South Africa he is asked Gwala Ka Jan? Which is the lingo for: Who are you? His or her answer will determine where he sleeps, who he associates with and where he sits in the prison hierarchy. Gwala Ka Jan is the name of a play developed by Pollsmoor offenders with the help of a creative writing teacher, Suzette Leal, who volunteered earlier this year at the prison, not quite knowing how drawn into the lives of individual convicts she would become. Nor did she know that the “narrative therapy” she was using would become not only a lifeline, but the foundation for a play, written by prisoners, starring prisoners and engaging an audience from outside of the prison walls. It’s not been done before in South Africa. To capture both the interaction between a relatively wealthy woman and three prisoners, as well as to explore the success of narrative therapy, we have been given permission to go inside Pollsmoor, under the watchful eye of Correctional Services. We have asked to interview three prisoners who are part of the play. Characters: • Curt Vincer, artist, recovering addict in prison for murdering his grandmother • Fareed Pelton, senior general of 27 gang, convicted murderer, serving time for breaking parole, trying to retire from the Number • Mdu, professional opera singer who is serving time for housebreaking (itv not quite guaranteed yet) They will talk about their backgrounds, what got them into prison, the impact of Narrative Therapy, and how the play has taken shape. They will talk of how they want the play to impact the audience, and the wider public. We will touch on the themes of identity, rehabilitation versus punishment and the tension between physical incarceration and imaginative freedom. We will ask them what it is like to be in prison, about their routines, and the world it creates around them. We will have to be sensitive of how much they want to tell us about the crimes they committed – I have been told that Curt is very sensitive and unsure whether he wants to reveal the whole story. We will also see them doing the things that make them special. We will film Curt drawing, and being the librarian at Medium B. I attach some of his pictures. We film Fareed writing in class with Suzette Leal who has engaged them in her class since March this year. We film Mdu singing. (Shades of the Shawshank Redemption) We will also film them all in dress rehearsal with Natasha Dryden, a former Sewende Laan actress who is helping them get the play ready. We will interview Natasha in the recreational hall once the dress rehearsal is done, so that she can reflect on what she is able to teach them and what she has experienced directing this play. We are obliged to interview a Correctional Services representative. They can’t decide who but will tell us in time as the person “needs to be prepared”. Correctional Services is in the process of trying to rebrand themselves as a more loving, caring rehabilitative institution. The week before the play, 300 warders and offenders are travelling to George (where John is) for a literary festival which will include a Spelling Bee in all the official languages, including Nama. I have asked for some visuals of this, to flesh out the theme of rehabilitation as opposed to punishment, as well as to strategically signal to DCS that we are on their side. Suzette tells me that most of the prisoners seem to while away their time sleeping, so the literary festival is in stark contrast to the default slumber. Then we will leave the prison to go “outside” to Camps Bay where Suzette lives. We will interview her there, and maybe get B-roll of her on the beach. I would want to capture visuals of “freedom” – beach, sea, palm trees in the wind etc as a contrast to the prison interior. Then we will return to Medium B on the night of one of the performances. I have asked for the camera to be back stage, to catch the nerves of the actors – those who can murder and housebreak but are nervous about standing up and saying their lines in front of an audience. We will capture them asking the audience the question: Gwala Ka Jan? and then also the applause at the end. This will make the shoot longer but seeing it is in the same week as our interviews, I think it is worth getting it. It should count as another half day. All of this has been signed off in principle by Correctional Services.
